title: Choosing a health care surrogate when estate planning
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Estate planning includes preparing for incapacitation. Anything might happen to you, making you unable to manage your affairs or make decisions for yourself. And one of those decisions is medical. An estate plan allows you to plan for such a possibility. Using a living will, you will outline your medical wishes regarding life-prolonging procedures. This…
content:
Estate planning includes preparing for incapacitation. Anything might happen to you, making you unable to manage your affairs or make decisions for yourself. And one of those decisions is medical.

An estate plan allows you to plan for such a possibility. Using a living will, you will outline your medical wishes regarding life-prolonging procedures. This includes instructions on the procedures that your physicians should provide, withhold or withdraw. You will then name a health care surrogate using the Designation of Health Care Surrogate document.

Your chosen surrogate will make medical decisions on your behalf. It’s important to choose a suitable party, given the sensitivity of the role they will assume. Here are four qualities to look out for:

Trustworthiness

Name someone you trust will follow your wishes and make decisions in your best interest. Note that you will also be granting the party access to your protected health information. Thus, trust is crucial.

Assertiveness

It helps to choose someone assertive. Someone who can ask doctors difficult questions, obtain more information about matters, handle conflicting opinions from family members and health care providers and speak up when instructions are not followed.

Calmness

If someone you know is always calm under stress and makes informed decisions fast, they possess one of the best qualities of a health care surrogate. Your chosen party will be required to make decisions during medical emergencies. You don’t want to name someone who will panic and delay making crucial decisions.

Proximity

Choosing someone who lives near you ensures they act fast during emergencies and makes it easier to have in-person meetings. Nonetheless, if a suitable party lives far away, you can make arrangements for travelling on short notice.

A health care surrogate plays a crucial role in your life. Learn more about identifying someone who will serve as expected.

title: Visa processing temporarily suspended
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: On Tuesday, August 25, the United States temporarily suspended its visa processing program. The reason given by the Department of State is that embassy and consular staff needed training regarding some of the new rules that will apply to both visas and green cards. They paused visa processing while this training took place. To a…
content:
On Tuesday, August 25, the United States temporarily suspended its visa processing program. The reason given by the Department of State is that embassy and consular staff needed training regarding some of the new rules that will apply to both visas and green cards. They paused visa processing while this training took place.

To a large degree, the new rules revolve around whether or not someone would need government benefits if they were permitted to live in the United States. These benefits were often provided for immigrants in the past, but the current government has been restricting travel to the country and instituting new rules to prevent government benefits from being given to certain immigrants.

This is similar to how, at the beginning of 2026, the government paused the processing of green cards for those from 75 specific countries. Even people who were already in the United States and had applied for a green card may not be approved if it appeared that they would receive certain types of government benefits.

Visa interviews have been canceled

In many cases, reports note that worldwide immigrant visa interviews have now been canceled due to this pause, and people in other countries are being prevented from entering the United States in the first place. Their visas are not being approved at this time.

These reports also note that it is unclear exactly when the processing of immigrant visas will resume. Some have noted that this may mean that certain visas could go to waste and will not be issued by September 30, which was the focus prior to this pause.

Changes to immigration laws, especially when it comes to visa and green card processing, can certainly complicate the process for immigrants. It is important for them to understand exactly what changes have taken place, what new rules may be used and what legal options they have.

title: What type of trust should you consider for your estate plan?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: A will is an essential estate planning document, but it may not accomplish everything you want. Assets distributed through a will generally must pass through probate, and a will may not provide enough control if you have minor children, a financially vulnerable beneficiary or property you want managed over time. A trust can complement your…
content:
A will is an essential estate planning document, but it may not accomplish everything you want. Assets distributed through a will generally must pass through probate, and a will may not provide enough control if you have minor children, a financially vulnerable beneficiary or property you want managed over time.

A trust can complement your will by allowing a trustee to hold and manage assets for your chosen beneficiaries. Depending on how it is structured, a trust may help your family avoid probate, protect an inheritance or carry out highly specific wishes. The right option depends on your assets, beneficiaries and long-term goals, but can include:

Revocable living trusts

A revocable living trust is created during your lifetime and can generally be changed or revoked as long as you remain mentally capable. You may serve as your own trustee and continue managing the property placed in the trust.

After your death, a successor trustee distributes or manages the trust property according to your instructions. Properly funded assets generally avoid probate. However, because you retain control over the trust, its assets are usually still considered yours for tax and creditor purposes.

Irrevocable trusts

An irrevocable trust is generally much harder to modify or revoke after it is established. In exchange for giving up some control, you may gain benefits that are not available through a revocable trust.

Depending on its structure and applicable law, an irrevocable trust may help with tax planning, asset protection, Medicaid planning or preserving property for future generations. These trusts are complex and should be created with careful legal and financial guidance.

Spendthrift trusts

A spendthrift trust may be useful when a beneficiary is not prepared to manage a large inheritance. Rather than receiving everything at once, the beneficiary can receive distributions according to terms established in the trust.

This arrangement may help protect assets from impulsive spending. It may also provide some protection against a beneficiary’s creditors, although the extent of that protection depends on state law and the trust’s language.

Incentive trusts

An incentive trust connects distributions to certain goals or conditions. For example, the trust might provide funds when a beneficiary reaches a particular age, earns a degree, purchases a home or maintains employment.

Conditions should be drafted carefully. Requirements that appear reasonable today could create unintended difficulties for a beneficiary whose health, abilities or circumstances later change.

Charitable trusts

A charitable trust can support a cause while also serving broader estate planning or tax goals. Some charitable trusts provide income to family members for a period before the remaining assets pass to a charity. Others pay a charity first and eventually transfer the remaining property to individual beneficiaries.

Choosing a trust requires more than selecting a name from a list. Professional legal guidance can help you determine whether a trust belongs in your estate plan and ensure that it is properly drafted and funded.

title: Do you need witnesses when establishing a power of attorney?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Under Florida law, the person establishing a power of attorney (the principal) needs to sign the document, and there must be two witnesses to this signature. Additionally, the document needs to be notarized by a notary public. Only when these official steps have been taken is the power of attorney (POA) properly established so that…
content:
Under Florida law, the person establishing a power of attorney (the principal) needs to sign the document, and there must be two witnesses to this signature. Additionally, the document needs to be notarized by a notary public. Only when these official steps have been taken is the power of attorney (POA) properly established so that it will be valid — allowing another person to act on behalf of the principal.

There are some potential exceptions to this rule. These could apply if it is a military power of attorney, for example, or if someone created a power of attorney while they were living in another state. In such a case, they may have been able to establish the document using those state-specific laws, which can differ from the laws of Florida.

Why are these steps so important?

These steps are necessary because a power of attorney is such a crucial document. Under normal circumstances, only an individual may have the legal right to make certain decisions or take actions on their own behalf. However, a power of attorney can be used to give these rights to someone else.

Exactly how the document is used will be unique from case to case. A power of attorney is often used to give another person access to financial accounts or the ability to work on a property transfer. It may also be used by a principal to give an agent authority to make medical decisions for them.

Florida does not take the shifting of these legal powers lightly, which is why the power of attorney needs to be properly established in order to be valid. If you are creating your estate plan or considering giving someone this authority, it is wise to have experienced legal guidance.

title: USCIS policy change on incomplete immigration benefit applications
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: A recent policy change has raised the stakes for immigrants filing applications for benefits with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Effective Aug. 5, 2026, USCIS officers may now broadly deny an application without first offering the individual the chance to correct any deficiencies. The underlying obligation on the applicant is not new: A person requesting…
content:
A recent policy change has raised the stakes for immigrants filing applications for benefits with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Effective Aug. 5, 2026, USCIS officers may now broadly deny an application without first offering the individual the chance to correct any deficiencies.

The underlying obligation on the applicant is not new: A person requesting an immigration benefit generally must establish their eligibility for that benefit and provide the required evidence when filing. The new policy merely decreases the likelihood that USCIS will ask for any missing information before simply issuing a denial.

The purpose of the change is to eliminate “placeholder” filings and frivolous claims, but it could have unfortunate consequences for applicants who make unintentional errors or misunderstand instructions.

An RFE or NOID is no longer expected

Previously, USCIS officers were encouraged to ask for more information whenever applicants submitted applications that were lacking enough information to prove their eligibility for a given benefit.

Typically, officers would issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) or a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID). An RFE tells the applicant or petitioner that USCIS needs additional evidence before making a decision. A NOID indicates that the agency intends to deny the request but provides an opportunity to respond. Either would give the applicant a chance to address an omission, clarify an issue or submit supporting documents so that their claim could proceed.

Now, under the updated policy, USCIS officers may still issue RFEs and NOIDs when they deem it appropriate, but it is no longer the established procedure. That means applicants should not assume that they will receive another opportunity to complete, correct or strengthen their claim if they make a mistake.

Complete preparation is more critical than ever

Before submitting an application for benefits, immigrants should carefully review the current application form, instructions and filing requirements, the evidence required to establish eligibility for the benefit as of the filing date and all their supporting documents.

Immigrating to the United States is becoming more challenging. Application denials can result in lost filing fees, delays and potentially serious consequences for one’s immigration journey. Anyone preparing a filing or concerned about an application that is already pending may benefit from legal guidance. The safest approach is to submit a complete, well-supported case from the beginning rather than relying on USCIS to request additional evidence later. Legal guidance is essential.

title: Which life changes may require estate plan changes?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Life rarely stays stagnant for long. As families grow, careers evolve and financial goals shift, the plans people made years ago may no longer completely reflect their current wishes. Many people create an estate plan and assume the work is finished. However, reviewing those documents after major life events can help ensure they continue to…
content:
Life rarely stays stagnant for long. As families grow, careers evolve and financial goals shift, the plans people made years ago may no longer completely reflect their current wishes.

Many people create an estate plan and assume the work is finished. However, reviewing those documents after major life events can help ensure they continue to protect loved ones and preserve personal wishes.

Major milestones that may change estate planning needs

An estate plan is a set of legal documents that explain how a person wants their assets, finances and care to be handled if they become incapacitated and after their death. An estate plan should change alongside life’s biggest milestones.

Marriage may mean adding a spouse to important documents or updating beneficiary designations. Divorce often requires removing an ex-spouse from certain roles and revisiting decisions about property distribution, powers of attorney and health care directives. The birth or adoption of a child is another important reason to review an estate plan, especially when choosing a guardian or creating trusts to manage future inheritances.

Retirement is another event that often signals it is time for an estate plan review. As people leave the workforce, their financial priorities frequently change, and retirement accounts may become a larger portion of their overall estate. It is also common for individuals to relocate after retirement, and estate planning laws can vary from state to state. Reviewing documents after moving or entering retirement can help ensure they remain legally effective and aligned with long-term goals.

Financial milestones deserve attention as well. Purchasing a home, starting a business, receiving an inheritance or experiencing significant investment growth can all affect how assets should be managed and transferred. A household’s financial circumstances can change significantly over time. As assets grow or become more complex, an outdated estate plan may no longer provide the protection or flexibility originally intended.

Estate planning is not a one-time task but an ongoing process that should reflect life’s changes. Speaking with an experienced legal professional after major milestones can help ensure important documents remain current, protect loved ones and continue to honor your wishes for the future.

title: What to know when naming a guardian for your child
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: If you have a minor child, it’s crucial to name a guardian for them. This is someone who will raise them to adulthood if you become unable to do so. In Florida, if the parents of a minor child become incapacitated or die without a named guardian, a judge appoints one. Therefore, it’s beneficial to…
content:
If you have a minor child, it’s crucial to name a guardian for them. This is someone who will raise them to adulthood if you become unable to do so.

In Florida, if the parents of a minor child become incapacitated or die without a named guardian, a judge appoints one. Therefore, it’s beneficial to choose that person yourself and codify that choice in your estate plan. Here are some important things to know when naming a guardian.

Have non-negotiable qualities

List qualities you believe a guardian should possess. For instance, choosing someone who shares your core values regarding parenting style, educational beliefs, morals and religion would help maintain stability for your child.

An existing bond can provide immediate emotional comfort for your child. Considering physical capacity to keep up with your child’s active routines can also be important. You should also consider the guardian’s location if you want your child to remain at their current school or in their neighborhood.

The two types of guardians

Florida law recognizes two primary categories of guardianship for a minor child. The guardian of the person lives with the child and makes day-to-day decisions. The guardian of the property manages the child’s financial assets. You can name one person to serve both roles, or you can name two people for each role.

It helps to name alternate guardians

An alternate guardian is a backup to the primary one. If a primary guardian is unable to serve when the time comes, an alternate is already named, so the court does not need to choose another guardian.

Parents of a minor child should name a guardian when estate planning. Get more information on how this and other estate planning steps can protect your child if you aren’t there to do so.

title: Who can serve as a personal representative in Florida?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: A personal representative administers a decedent’s probate estate. Some of their duties include securing, valuing and managing the estate’s assets, communicating with beneficiaries and interested parties, paying debts and taxes, distributing assets to beneficiaries and closing the estate. If you are estate planning, you should name a party who can perform these duties competently. You…
content:
A personal representative administers a decedent’s probate estate. Some of their duties include securing, valuing and managing the estate’s assets, communicating with beneficiaries and interested parties, paying debts and taxes, distributing assets to beneficiaries and closing the estate.

If you are estate planning, you should name a party who can perform these duties competently. You can name a person, bank or trust company.

If you nominate an individual, the judge who will be in charge of your estate’s administration will appoint them when the time comes. To be appointed, your chosen party must be:

Above 18 years

A minor cannot be appointed as a personal representative in Florida since they lack the legal capacity to be bound by or held liable for fiduciary contracts.

Mentally and physically capable to perform duties

A personal representative must be mentally and physically able to perform the required duties to be appointed. And such capacity must continue throughout the administration. If an appointed personal representative becomes physically or mentally incapacitated while administering the estate, the court can remove them from the role.

A Florida resident or a close relative of the deceased

Florida requires personal representatives to be legal residents of the state. An out-of-state nominated party can only be appointed if they are a spouse, sibling, parent, child or other close relative of the decedent.

Free of felony convictions

An individual who has been convicted of a felony cannot be appointed as a personal representative in Florida.

Are there restrictions for banks and trust companies?

A trust company or bank is entitled to act as a personal representative if it’s authorized and qualified to exercise fiduciary powers in Florida.

When estate planning, you need to confirm that the party you want to name as your estate’s personal representative will be appointed by the court. Learn more to make an informed decision.

title: Should my fiancée come to the USA to get a green card?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: It seems like the sensible choice, i.e., bringing your fiancée here to the United States to let her apply for a green card and make her your wife. But like many areas of the immigration process, the recent policy changes affect the choices being made at all levels. Under current immigration policies (which may or…
content:
It seems like the sensible choice, i.e., bringing your fiancée here to the United States to let her apply for a green card and make her your wife. But like many areas of the immigration process, the recent policy changes affect the choices being made at all levels.

Under current immigration policies (which may or may not face judicial pushback), it may not be wise to bring your fiancée here to the States to apply for residency status.

Could changes affect marriage plans?

They might. If you and your beloved intend to exchange vows in person here in the USA, the most recent immigration policy changes might preclude your carrying out your plans. However, you could still marry by traveling to their country of origin or elsewhere and marrying. Then, they could pursue their case for a green card from afar.

What about spouses who aren’t citizens?

This group may also experience changes to their immigration status under the changes, which took effect this month. Administration officials have stated that greater scrutiny will be given to these permanent residency cases, with approval granted only on a case-by-case basis.

Confusion is understandable

If you are an immigrant or are engaged to or married to one, being confused about the recent changes and their implications is to be expected. You might also hear rumors that may or may not be rooted in reality.

Trust your legal advocate to help you stay abreast of the changes that affect your immigration status and the rights of your loved one to remain here in the United States. Knowledge is power, so stay strong and aware of your options.

title: The test requirements for naturalization
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Naturalization is the process that allows a foreign national living in the United States to become a citizen. Lawful permanent residents who have resided in the country for years can apply for naturalization. Provided that they pass a background check and meet all of the criteria imposed by the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services…
content:
Naturalization is the process that allows a foreign national living in the United States to become a citizen. Lawful permanent residents who have resided in the country for years can apply for naturalization.

Provided that they pass a background check and meet all of the criteria imposed by the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), they can schedule a naturalization interview. During that interview, they not only answer questions but must also pass tests.

Understanding the testing requirements can help immigrants improve their chances of successfully naturalizing.

There are typically two mandatory tests

Immigrants hoping to become citizens must pass two specific tests in addition to meeting all other standards. The USCIS administers an English language test and a Civics test.

The language test requires demonstrations of reading and writing, as well as the ability to speak in English and comprehend spoken English. The Civics test is an oral test that involves 20 questions about the history and government of the United States. Applicants must answer at least 12 of the 20 questions correctly to pass.

There are accommodations available for immigrants with disabling medical conditions. There are also English language exemptions available for immigrants who are over a certain age and have years of lawful residence in the United States. Seeking accommodations or exemptions can help people pass the tests necessary to become naturalized citizens.

Preparing for the test requires practicing English skills and studying the 128 questions that could be on the Civics test. Immigrants may also need help with paperwork as they prepare for naturalization. Those hoping to become citizens often need the support of an attorney as they prepare for naturalization interviews and the tests, and that’s okay.

title: Helping foreign siblings to secure green cards
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: People who immigrate to the United States can improve their lives. They may have more economic opportunities and can protect themselves from persecution abroad. They may start businesses, get married and build community ties. Those who have settled into new lives in the United States may want to share their good fortune with their closest…
content:
People who immigrate to the United States can improve their lives. They may have more economic opportunities and can protect themselves from persecution abroad. They may start businesses, get married and build community ties.

Those who have settled into new lives in the United States may want to share their good fortune with their closest loved ones, especially if they couldn’t travel with them when they first entered the country. Immigration rules prioritize immediate family members. However, there are systems in place that allow other relatives to obtain visas. In addition to assisting spouses and children, immigrants can sometimes help their brothers or sisters living abroad legally enter the United States.

Who has the option of helping a sibling obtain a green card?

Only citizens can sponsor siblings

People hoping to qualify for family-based immigration opportunities are subject to the same background checks and medical standards as any other immigrant. Those living abroad hoping to acquire a visa or green card through a sibling relationship must submit medical records and pass a comprehensive background check. They also typically need to have documentation validating their relationship with a citizen.

Restrictions on family immigration are one reason to consider naturalization. Permanent residents who become naturalized citizens can help their siblings and parents enter the United States. They can also sponsor their children for immigration after they marry. Permanent residents with green cards can only offer opportunities to their spouses and unmarried children.

Under certain circumstances, siblings of citizens can potentially become permanent residents and may eventually become citizens as well. Reviewing family immigration goals with an attorney can help people explore their options.

title: Will you risk deportation if you get divorced?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: It is natural to feel concerned about deportation if you have a green card based on your marriage. Your spouse is already a citizen, and you are a permanent resident specifically because the two of you are married. If you file for divorce, you may worry that this will invalidate your status and lead to…
content:
It is natural to feel concerned about deportation if you have a green card based on your marriage. Your spouse is already a citizen, and you are a permanent resident specifically because the two of you are married. If you file for divorce, you may worry that this will invalidate your status and lead to deportation.

As a general rule, however, this is not a concern you need to have. For most people, getting divorced will not affect their status. You are not going to be deported just because your marriage ended.

The main issue that you may face is if the government believes that your relationship was not authentic the entire time. If a quick divorce makes it seem like you only got married and pretended to be in a relationship to get the green card, then it could be a problem. But if you were genuinely in a relationship that is now coming to an end, you should not have to worry.

Domestic violence issues

In some cases, people are seeking to end their relationship because they are experiencing domestic violence from their spouse.

If you are in this situation, then it is important to know that you can sometimes get a domestic violence green card. You are able to self-petition for this card, meaning you do not have to feel trapped in your marriage just because you think it is going to affect your immigration status.

Carefully considering your future

Marital status, immigration status and other such issues can have a dramatic impact on your future in the United States. As you navigate this complex process, make sure you know exactly what legal options you have and what steps you will need to take.

title: Can you study for your green card marriage interview?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: No, you cannot study for a green card marriage interview. There is nothing to prepare for in advance, as you would with other important immigration steps. If you are seeking to become a naturalized citizen, for example, you certainly can study and prepare yourself to provide the necessary answers regarding how the U.S. government works…
content:
No, you cannot study for a green card marriage interview. There is nothing to prepare for in advance, as you would with other important immigration steps. If you are seeking to become a naturalized citizen, for example, you certainly can study and prepare yourself to provide the necessary answers regarding how the U.S. government works and things of this nature. But a green card marriage interview is much different.

During this interview, you and your spouse are simply going to be asked questions about your relationship and your daily life together. For instance, the interviewer may ask when the two of you met, where you had your wedding, what roles and responsibilities you have around the house or even simple things like where you like to go to dinner together.

What is the goal of the interview?

The thing to keep in mind is that the goal of this interview is just to demonstrate that you are in a real relationship. The government wants to get a sense of authenticity, rather than specific answers.

If they ask where the two of you met and you both give drastically different answers, for example, that is a red flag. They may believe that you are just pretending to be in a relationship in order to get a green card.

So, rather than preparing any of your answers in advance or studying specific topics, it is best to answer honestly and truthfully about your life together, demonstrating that the two of you are in an authentic relationship and that a green card will allow that to continue.

Navigating the immigration process

Getting a green card is an important step to take, but it may just be one of many that you consider during your immigration journey. It can help to work with an experienced attorney at this time.

title: What is an anatomical gift declaration?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Thinking about the future often involves making decisions that reflect our values and wishes. Estate planning allows us to put those decisions in writing so our loved ones have guidance when important moments eventually arise. Some estate planning documents focus on finances, property and healthcare decisions. Others address personal choices, including what happens after death…
content:
Thinking about the future often involves making decisions that reflect our values and wishes. Estate planning allows us to put those decisions in writing so our loved ones have guidance when important moments eventually arise.

Some estate planning documents focus on finances, property and healthcare decisions. Others address personal choices, including what happens after death and whether we wish to help others through organ and tissue donation.

Understanding anatomical gifts

An anatomical gift is a donation of organs, tissues, eyes or the body after death. Advances in medicine have made it possible to transplant more than 25 different human organs and tissues, helping save lives and improve the health of countless individuals. Anatomical gifts may also be used for medical research, education and other purposes permitted by law.

Many people are familiar with registering as an organ donor through their driver’s license. However, Florida law recognizes several ways to document these wishes, including donor registration, advance directives and other written instruments. Taking steps to clearly express these preferences can help ensure they are understood and honored.

An anatomical gift differs from other estate planning documents because it focuses specifically on the donation of organs and tissues after death. For example, a will generally addresses the distribution of property and assets, while a healthcare directive outlines medical treatment preferences during a person’s lifetime. An anatomical gift serves a separate purpose by documenting a person’s wishes regarding organ, tissue or body donation.

Individuals may choose to donate specific organs or tissues, authorize donations for transplantation or research, or make broader decisions about how their donation may be used. Discussing these wishes with family members can help reduce uncertainty and provide guidance during a difficult time.

Estate planning often involves several documents working together to create a comprehensive plan. For those who wish to leave a lasting impact through donation, including their wishes regarding anatomical gifts, can be an important part of that process. Speaking with an experienced legal professional can help ensure estate planning documents reflect personal goals and comply with state laws.

title: The green card application process has just dramatically changed
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Immigration policies have shifted in several ways lately. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has recently released a memo that could affect people hoping to obtain a green card through adjustment of status. Traditionally, many people who were legally present in the United States on temporary visas, including student visas, tourist visas and temporary work…
content:
Immigration policies have shifted in several ways lately. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has recently released a memo that could affect people hoping to obtain a green card through adjustment of status.

Traditionally, many people who were legally present in the United States on temporary visas, including student visas, tourist visas and temporary work visas, could apply for lawful permanent residence from within the country through the adjustment of status process if they qualified through employment, family sponsorship or marriage to a U.S. citizen.

Under the new guidance, USCIS now describes adjustment of status – which allows immigrants already in the United States to apply for green cards without leaving the country – as an “extraordinary” form of relief rather than the ordinary path to permanent residency for many applicants. Officers are being instructed to treat consular processing abroad as the default option.

While the memo does not completely eliminate adjustment of status applications from within U.S. borders, it is unclear what “extraordinary circumstances” might allow for that method. The guidance remains vague in several areas, leaving many applicants and employers uncertain about how the policy will be applied in practice.

A significant disruption to the immigration process for many

Leaving and returning to the USA can be expensive and inconvenient. These applications can often take considerable time, and the result is never guaranteed, so that could prove a significant disruption to the life an immigrant was already building here. In some situations, applicants who leave the country could also face additional immigration complications or delays before being allowed to return.

For example, a worker in the United States on an employment visa may have an employer prepared to sponsor them for permanent residency. If the employee must leave the country for an uncertain period while the application is processed overseas, the disruption may affect both the worker and the employer’s long-term plans.

A USCIS spokesperson said they are merely “returning to the original intent of the law.” The fact remains that the interpretation outlined in the memo represents a significant change in how the law has been applied, and it could complicate matters and increase costs and uncertainty for many who hoped to apply for a green card via adjustment of status. It is almost certain that legal challenges to the new rules will occur.

Experienced legal guidance is advisable to understand how best to navigate the green card application process, whether you are an applicant or hoping to sponsor someone. Because immigration policies and enforcement priorities are constantly shifting, it is more important than ever to stay carefully informed and strategic about every step.

title: Estate planning for Floridians with non-citizen spouses
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Many Florida residents are in “mixed status” marriages where one spouse is a U.S. citizen and the other isn’t. Often, people think that they can’t include their non-citizen spouse as a beneficiary in their estate plan, even though they are here legally – usually as a green card holder. Non-citizen spouses can indeed be included…
content:
Many Florida residents are in “mixed status” marriages where one spouse is a U.S. citizen and the other isn’t. Often, people think that they can’t include their non-citizen spouse as a beneficiary in their estate plan, even though they are here legally – usually as a green card holder.

Non-citizen spouses can indeed be included as beneficiaries. However, there can be significant tax consequences if an estate is large enough that it’s subject to federal estate tax.

When one spouse passes away, the surviving spouse gets a 100% marital deduction of estate tax – but only if they’re a U.S. citizen. That’s why many people wait for their spouse to complete the process of becoming a citizen to put an estate plan in place. Unfortunately, that delay can have serious consequences for their spouse and the rest of their family if they die unexpectedly. Further, some non-citizen spouses have no interest in becoming U.S. citizens.

What is a QDOT?

That’s where a qualified domestic trust (QDOT) comes in. It lets a non-citizen surviving spouse take advantage of the 100% marital deduction. Let’s look at how a QDOT works and why it’s recommended for those with non-citizen spouses.

  • Assets are placed in a QDOT for which the spouse is the sole beneficiary
  • The trust can provide income for the surviving spouse
  • A trustee (and successor trustee), both U.S. citizens, are appointed

Note that if an entity like a bank or trust company is the trustee, it must be a qualified domestic corporation.

A QDOT isn’t necessary for everyone who has a non-citizen spouse. However, even if you don’t anticipate having an estate that will be subject to federal estate tax, it’s a good idea to know about this option – and more importantly, to know how to best plan for your spouse and the rest of your family after you’re gone. That’s where having sound estate planning guidance can make all the difference.

title: The importance of regular estate plan reviews
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Creating an estate plan is something every adult should do sooner rather than later. This is true even if they do not have much to pass on. Once the initial creation of the plan is done, they should set themselves a calendar reminder to review it every couple of years. When a plan is no…
content:
Creating an estate plan is something every adult should do sooner rather than later. This is true even if they do not have much to pass on.

Once the initial creation of the plan is done, they should set themselves a calendar reminder to review it every couple of years. When a plan is no longer up to date, it may fail to achieve what they hope and could create problems for themselves or others down the line. Here are some typical reasons that people need to update their estate plan.

A change in marital status

Marrying or divorcing someone will likely involve changing your beneficiaries. It could also alter what you own. You do not want your beneficiaries wasting time wondering where an asset destined for them in your will is when you ceded it to your ex-spouse in the divorce.

A change in who you want to fulfill roles

A thorough estate plan will name people to certain roles, such as executor, power of attorney and guardian of minor children. You may need to replace these people because they die or become unavailable, such as if they move far away. You may choose to change them because you no longer feel they are the best person for the role.

A change in those you wish to receive assets

Perhaps you never married and were planning to leave the contents of your estate to the local animal shelter when you died. Then, your neighbor had a child, whom you grew increasingly fond of over time to the point you would now like to leave some of your estate to them to help with their college education. If you do not make that change in your estate plan, it simply won’t happen.

Those are just some of the scenarios in which you might want to amend your estate plan. It’s something that is easy to forget to do. Regularly scheduling time to review your estate plan every couple of years may be the reminder you need to make and codify those changes while you still can.

title: 3 things that could jeopardize your green card renewal
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Once you succeed in getting a green card, that’s not the end of the process. You will need to renew it when required. While renewal is a relatively straightforward process for many people, that’s not a guarantee. The immigration authorities can reject an application for renewal and with it your right to stay in the…
content:
Once you succeed in getting a green card, that’s not the end of the process. You will need to renew it when required. While renewal is a relatively straightforward process for many people, that’s not a guarantee.

The immigration authorities can reject an application for renewal and with it your right to stay in the U.S. Here are some reasons this could happen.

Doubt over your actual residency

A green card gives you the right to reside in the U.S. However, unlike citizenship, where you can come and go as you please, you must continue to be a resident here. That means paying your taxes here and living here most of the time.

One reason people lose their green card is that they need to go back home for a considerable period to care for a sick relative, which often prolongs their stay more than they initially thought. When they go to renew their green card, the authorities say they have not been in the U.S. enough to retain it.

Doubt over the veracity of your original application

If the immigration authorities convince a court that your original green card application was fraudulent, then you can retroactively lose your permanent residency status. This is true even if many years have passed since you submitted that application.

One reason this might occur is if a genuine marriage, which enabled you to get a green card, quickly ended in divorce. That can cause the authorities to believe that the marriage was not entered into with legitimate intentions.

Missing the renewal date

Life can get busy, and most people forget the odd important date. Your green card renewal is not a date you can afford to forget. If you miss the date, your renewal application will likely be rejected.

Seeking experienced legal guidance well ahead of time gives you a better chance of avoiding or dealing with any issues that could hinder your green card renewal.

title: The importance of estate planning
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Many people procrastinate estate planning, sometimes because they do not understand exactly how important it is. This keeps them from making it a priority. The truth is that there are many potential benefits to estate planning. Additionally, procrastination is a significant gamble because you could pass away without ever putting a plan in place. Below…
content:
Many people procrastinate estate planning, sometimes because they do not understand exactly how important it is. This keeps them from making it a priority.

The truth is that there are many potential benefits to estate planning. Additionally, procrastination is a significant gamble because you could pass away without ever putting a plan in place. Below are a few of the key benefits of drafting a plan this year.

Your wishes will be followed

First and foremost, state law takes precedence if you pass away without an estate plan, and some key decisions may have to be made by family members. There is no telling if this will line up with what you want. By leaving your family an estate plan, you ensure that your actual wishes will be followed.

Avoiding estate disputes

A plan can also help avoid estate disputes between beneficiaries. They can read the documentation and know precisely what you wanted, so they do not have to make decisions on their own, reducing the chances of conflict.

Protection for minor children

If you have minor children, an estate plan is very important to protect their future. You could put assets in a trust to hold for them when they grow older, for example, and choose a guardian who can take on a parental role in their lives if you pass away unexpectedly.

Considering your medical future

Finally, estate planning can focus on your own medical future. You can make decisions in advance with a living will, or you can use a power of attorney to choose an agent to make those decisions on your behalf.

These are just a few reasons why estate planning is important. Take the time to carefully look at all of your legal options and draft a plan that will work for you and your family.

title: Conditional approval of a marriage green card
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Marriage is one of the most common ways for people to seek a green card in the United States. It can also be one of the fastest. The government does prioritize issuing green cards to married couples so that both people are allowed to stay together in the United States. However, there are some cases…
content:
Marriage is one of the most common ways for people to seek a green card in the United States. It can also be one of the fastest. The government does prioritize issuing green cards to married couples so that both people are allowed to stay together in the United States.

However, there are some cases in which a person will only get conditional approval. One example is if you apply for your green card, but you have only been married to a U.S. citizen – who is petitioning on your behalf – for less than two years. You can still file Form I-485, but you may only be granted conditional approval based on the short duration of your marriage.

How long will this last?

Your conditional status will last for two years after the green card is issued. You can then take steps to have that status removed.

In order to do this, you need to file Form I-751. There are important deadlines that must be met. Typically, you need to file this form 90 days before the expiration of your conditional residence.

As with other immigration issues, meeting these specific deadlines is important, as you may lose the opportunity to file or have your claim denied, even if you otherwise would have made a valid request that would have been approved.

Filing the proper paperwork

To ensure that you know exactly what forms to file and when to do so to streamline your immigration process, it can help to work with an experienced attorney, whether you are interested in obtaining a visa, going through naturalization, adjusting your status or any other aspect of this process.

title: 3 mistakes that can jeopardize your K-1 visa
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: If you and your partner are looking to start your life together in the United States, applying for a K-1 visa or fiancé(e) visa is likely one of your first big steps. This visa allows your foreign partner to enter the U.S. so you can marry within 90 days of arrival. The process can be…
content:
If you and your partner are looking to start your life together in the United States, applying for a K-1 visa or fiancé(e) visa is likely one of your first big steps. This visa allows your foreign partner to enter the U.S. so you can marry within 90 days of arrival.

The process can be exciting, but it’s also complicated and detail-heavy. Even small errors can derail your application, which is why it helps to understand the common pitfalls to avoid. Here are some of the mistakes that trip up many K-1 visa applicants.

1. Incomplete or inconsistent paperwork

The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) doesn’t chase down missing documents. If anything is absent, incorrect or inconsistent in the paperwork you submit, your case gets delayed or returned. Pay close attention to dates, spelling of names and supporting evidence. Even one mismatched birthdate can send your file to the back of the line.

2. Weak evidence of your relationship

USCIS wants proof that your relationship is genuine. Otherwise, your application is likely to be unsuccessful. Generic letters or screenshots of social media posts may not be enough. Include photographs, travel itineraries, chat logs and communication that demonstrates your ongoing relationship. Solid evidence can make the difference between approval and denial.

3. Overlooking crucial deadlines

Meeting important timelines is critical in the K-1 visa process. From scheduling your consulate interview to responding promptly to USCIS requests, delays can slow your case or even lead to complications. Mark all key dates on your calendar and respond promptly to any USCIS requests.

It’s also worth noting that you have 90 days to finalize your marriage once your partner arrives in the U.S. Missing this can create additional legal hurdles.

Don’t risk your future together

The K-1 visa journey can quickly become overwhelming due to the complex paperwork, strict deadlines and legal nuances involved in the process. Seeking professional legal guidance early in the process can help you do everything right and increase the chances of a smooth, timely approval.

title: Skipping a living will can put your family in a tough spot
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Most people know that planning ahead for their healthcare is important, yet still put off creating a living will. This legal document ensures your healthcare preferences are followed if you’re ever unable to speak for yourself. One reason many people avoid making a living will is that it brings attention to uncomfortable scenarios they’d rather…
content:
Most people know that planning ahead for their healthcare is important, yet still put off creating a living will. This legal document ensures your healthcare preferences are followed if you’re ever unable to speak for yourself.

One reason many people avoid making a living will is that it brings attention to uncomfortable scenarios they’d rather not consider. Planning for incapacitation or serious medical decisions can feel overwhelming, and discussing medical preferences with family may seem awkward or tense. On top of that, the legal aspects can appear complicated, making it easy to delay.

What happens if you don’t have one?

Without a living will, someone else will have to step in and make critical medical decisions on your behalf. It could be your next of kin or a court-appointed individual, which can lead to unnecessary complications. For instance, family members may disagree on what you would have wanted, which can delay treatment and create emotional strain.

In some cases, these disagreements can even escalate to legal disputes, adding stress and potential costs that could have been avoided. Your silence can become someone else’s burden, and it’s your family who’ll bear the brunt of it all.

Acting now matters

Taking the time to create a living will is one of the most impactful steps you can take to protect your interests and spare your loved ones the difficult responsibility of making sensitive medical decisions. Since a living will is a legally enforceable document, your family members or healthcare providers must follow the instructions you’ve clearly laid out.

If you’re unsure of where to begin or how you can craft a comprehensive living will, reaching out for qualified legal guidance can help you take proper steps and ensure every detail is handled correctly. The peace of mind that comes with knowing your wishes will be honored, and your family won’t face unnecessary stress or uncertainty is priceless.

title: How long until you can become a U.S. citizen?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: The path to U.S. citizenship, or naturalization, is typically a long one. Often, you need to get a green card and spend a certain amount of time as a permanent resident before you can begin the naturalization process. For many people, the overall process starts even earlier, as they may initially enter the United States…
content:
The path to U.S. citizenship, or naturalization, is typically a long one. Often, you need to get a green card and spend a certain amount of time as a permanent resident before you can begin the naturalization process. For many people, the overall process starts even earlier, as they may initially enter the United States on a visa, then get a green card, and then apply for citizenship.

But exactly how long is it going to take? If you already have your green card, how long do you need to wait until you can become a citizen?

Your relationship status

As a general rule, you need to be in the U.S. on a green card for five years. Only after you have satisfied this requirement can you work on becoming a citizen, which would allow you to stay permanently.

However, your relationship status plays a major role. If you are married to someone who is already a U.S. citizen, your path to citizenship becomes shorter. You only need to remain in the U.S. on a green card for three years before you are able to apply.

Of course, the citizenship process itself can also take time, so it is not an overnight shift from one status to the other. You will need to know what forms are required and what other documentation is necessary, beyond simply establishing yourself as a permanent resident for a certain amount of time. But it is important to understand the general timeframe so that you know what to expect.

Becoming a U.S. citizen

If you are interested in citizenship, it can be a major step for your life and your future. Be sure that you are well aware of the necessary legal steps that are required under U.S. law.

title: Can you travel outside of the U.S. while on a green card?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: When you become a permanent resident of the United States, you are given a green card. This establishes your status and allows you to lawfully live and work in the country without the requirement that you have a specific visa, such as an employment visa. However, you may be worried about certain actions putting your…
content:
When you become a permanent resident of the United States, you are given a green card. This establishes your status and allows you to lawfully live and work in the country without the requirement that you have a specific visa, such as an employment visa.

However, you may be worried about certain actions putting your status in jeopardy. If you travel abroad, leaving the United States for a certain period of time, could that cause problems with your green card in the future? Would you be putting your permanent resident status at risk?

Short-term travel versus abandoning your status

Typically speaking, there is not an issue with short-term travel plans. If you simply want to go on vacation or spend a week visiting family who live abroad, it does not put your permanent resident status in jeopardy.

However, if you travel out of the country for an extended period of time, the government may determine that you have abandoned your status or that you never intended to make the United States your permanent home in the first place. If you obtain a green card as a permanent resident of the U.S. but spend most of your time living abroad, that status could be revoked.

Although every situation is unique, a general rule of thumb is that you should not leave the country for more than one year. If you need to do so, you should first use Form I-131, which is an application for a reentry permit. If you have this permit, you may be able to take an extended trip, but still re-enter the country without losing your green card.

Your legal rights

Immigration law can be very complicated, and it is important to understand your rights and how they can affect your status. It can help to work with an experienced attorney at this time.

title: Selecting a successor trustee for a living revocable trust
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: There are numerous benefits that people can derive when they establish revocable living trusts. One of the perks, when compared with an irrevocable trust, is the ability to act as the initial trustee. The person funding the trust can manage trust resources until they die or become incapacitated. At that point, the successor trustee they…
content:
There are numerous benefits that people can derive when they establish revocable living trusts. One of the perks, when compared with an irrevocable trust, is the ability to act as the initial trustee. The person funding the trust can manage trust resources until they die or become incapacitated.

At that point, the successor trustee they selected assumes responsibility over ongoing trust administration. Choosing an appropriate candidate to serve as successor trustee can be a challenge, especially for those concerned about family conflict after their passing.

How do trustors choose the right person to serve as their successor trustee?

Availability and capability are key

Selecting a successor trustee requires a careful assessment of an individual’s capabilities. A trustee must be organized and able to follow complex instructions. They may need to manage and distribute a variety of valuable assets.

They may need to manage conflict well, as family members and other interested parties may question their management or the instructions for trust administration. Selecting someone who is reliable and ethical is of the utmost importance.

An individual’s availability to manage trust administration is also a key consideration. The most capable individuals in a person’s inner circle might have demanding careers or family responsibilities that diminish their ability to manage the trust. They may live far enough away to make hands-on management of resources impractical.

Individuals establishing revocable living trusts may want to create a list of candidates and review their options with the attorney assisting them with the creation of the trust. Choosing an appropriate successor trustee helps protect an individual when they are vulnerable and ensures that their trust has a positive impact on their legacy.

title: 3 benefits of drafting a lady bird deed for a Florida residence
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Lady bird deeds, also known as enhanced life estate deeds, are highly useful but relatively uncommon estate planning tools. They are uncommon in part because only five states currently allow their use. Florida is one of those states. Property owners planning for the future of their residences may benefit from drafting a lady bird deed…
content:
Lady bird deeds, also known as enhanced life estate deeds, are highly useful but relatively uncommon estate planning tools. They are uncommon in part because only five states currently allow their use. Florida is one of those states.

Property owners planning for the future of their residences may benefit from drafting a lady bird deed that grants them control of the property now and allows for the transfer of the property to a beneficiary in the future. What are the common benefits associated with a lady bird deed?

1. Bypassing probate

When an owner’s interest in real property is part of their estate, it must pass through probate court. There may be a significant delay in the final transfer of ownership. Their beneficiary might wait years. Lady bird deeds bypass probate and speed up the transfer of ownership to the selected beneficiary.

2. Medicaid protections

Lady bird deeds offer benefits to adults who believe they may require Medicaid for long-term care. They do not need to worry about losing equity to estate recovery efforts after their death. A deed executed years before an owner needs Medicaid benefits can protect their equity from estate recovery claims.

3. Financial protection for beneficiaries

The owner who drafts a lady bird deed agrees to limit their use of the property for the remainder of their life. Specifically, they generally cannot sell or give away the property, as the beneficiary is now a co-owner with protected legal rights.

People who intend to have their homes passed to a specific person after they die may want to consider adding a lady bird deed to their estate plans. The right documents can help limit the loss of home equity and speed up the transfer of ownership.

title: Are you ready for your Stokes interview?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: One of the traditional tools that the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has used to deter fraudulent marriages is the Stokes interview. Those attempting to get a green card because of their marriage to a United States citizen often face increased scrutiny. Stokes interviews are usually pivotal to the approval process, so it…
content:
One of the traditional tools that the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has used to deter fraudulent marriages is the Stokes interview. Those attempting to get a green card because of their marriage to a United States citizen often face increased scrutiny.

Stokes interviews are usually pivotal to the approval process, so it pays to go into your Stokes interview fully prepared. Below is some important information for those seeking green cards through marriage.

A Stokes interview is the second round

If you initially failed to convince the USCIS officer screening your case of the legitimacy of your marriage, you will get notified to attend a Stokes interview. Think of it as a second chance to make a good impression. Hence, the need to prepare ahead of time.

However, today, more USCIS officers are exercising their right to include Stokes interviews during the first interview, so it’s prudent to stay prepared all throughout the process.

The questions get granular

While some questions are mundane and expected, e.g., “Where did you meet?” or “Describe your first date?”, others get downright personal. They might ask who sleeps on which side of the bed or even what method the couple uses for birth control.

It’s a good idea to review the list of questions with your spouse so there are no surprises.

Be prepared but not rehearsed

While you certainly don’t want to be blindsided by these questions, you also don’t want to sound rehearsed or as if the answers were memorized and not organic. By working closely with your legal team during the immigration process, you may be able to eliminate some stumbling blocks.

title: Choosing a guardian for your minor child when estate planning
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: If you have a minor child, it’s critical to name a guardian for them when estate planning. This ensures they have someone who will take care of them if you are unable to because of incapacitation or death. It’s important to determine the most suitable person for this role. Below are two aspects to consider…
content:
If you have a minor child, it’s critical to name a guardian for them when estate planning. This ensures they have someone who will take care of them if you are unable to because of incapacitation or death. It’s important to determine the most suitable person for this role.

Below are two aspects to consider when making your selection:

Willingness and qualities of potential guardians

Chances are, you have a few loved ones who can raise your child to adulthood. To pick one, you need first to consider willingness. Have separate meetings with your potential parties to inform them of your wish. Then, detail the role, lifestyle changes and financial responsibilities. Doing this helps you narrow down to parties who are willing to serve as your minor child’s guardian.

The next step will be assessing their qualities. These include physical and mental health, shared values and financial stability, among others. You want to choose a guardian who satisfactorily meets the qualities you believe are necessary to raise your child as you would have.

Types of guardianships

There are two types of guardianship for a minor child in Florida: guardianship of the person and guardianship of the property.

The former type appoints someone to make personal decisions for a minor child, such as daily care, education and medical, whereas the latter type appoints someone to make financial decisions, for example, when a minor child receives an inheritance, insurance proceeds or a lawsuit settlement.

When estate planning, you can name two parties for these roles, or one person can be a combination of both. Assess the qualities of your potential parties to make an informed decision.

Naming a guardian for your minor child is an important step in estate planning. Get more information on how you can considerably protect your child.

title: What happens if you lose your job while on an employment visa?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: The U.S. Department of State stopped issuing immigrant visas for nationals from 75 countries on Jan. 21, 2026. This new rule halts green card processing at U.S. embassies abroad. Officials say they need time to review how they screen for public charge risks. The government wants to block entry for individuals who might become primarily…
content:
The U.S. Department of State stopped issuing immigrant visas for nationals from 75 countries on Jan. 21, 2026. This new rule halts green card processing at U.S. embassies abroad. Officials say they need time to review how they screen for public charge risks. The government wants to block entry for individuals who might become primarily dependent on public benefits. Applicants may still go to interviews. However, consular officers cannot issue immigrant visas until further notice.

Which countries face the visa pause?

The Department of State stopped visa issuance for 75 countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe. This list includes nations such as Afghanistan, Brazil, Egypt, Iran, Nigeria, Russia and Thailand. The government chose countries it views as high risk for potential public charge inadmissibility. A person can check their status with the Department of State or an attorney.

The visa pause impacts several categories of applicants:

  • Family members who want to join relatives in the U.S.
  • Workers waiting for green cards through an employer
  • Diversity Visa winners who do not have their stamps yet

This policy marks a major change in how the government handles entry rules.

How does the public charge test affect applicants?

The public charge review checks if an applicant is likely to depend on the government for subsistence. Consular officers now look closely at an applicant’s age, health and financial assets. They also check job skills and English proficiency. Past use of public aid is a negative factor.

Officers use specific criteria for most immigrant cases:

  • Health reviews now cover long-term illnesses such as diabetes
  • Income checks focus on the assets a sponsor holds
  • Large families face heightened scrutiny because they require higher income thresholds

These strict rules ensure new residents can pay for their own needs.

Does the 2026 pause affect travel visas?

This move only affects immigrant visas. It does not stop travel or work visas. Tourist, student and H-1B visas stay active. Even so, travelers should expect more questions about their finances during interviews. Applicants should carry evidence of financial self-sufficiency.

The legal path for all travelers is changing:

  • Wait times at consulates in these 75 countries will likely grow
  • Proof of resources must show independent financial stability
  • Interview rules focus on strict vetting

The pause does not apply to individuals applying with a second passport from a non-listed nation. Understanding these shifts is a key part of managing an ongoing immigration law case.

title: When are immigrants at risk of denaturalization?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: For many immigrants, naturalization is the final step in the process of becoming an American citizen. After entering the country with a visa and then obtaining a green card, they eventually pursue citizenship. Naturalized citizens have the same rights as natural-born citizens. They can vote, work without prior authorization, sponsor family members for immigration opportunities…
content:
For many immigrants, naturalization is the final step in the process of becoming an American citizen. After entering the country with a visa and then obtaining a green card, they eventually pursue citizenship.

Naturalized citizens have the same rights as natural-born citizens. They can vote, work without prior authorization, sponsor family members for immigration opportunities and even run for most political offices. However, there is one key difference.

Naturalized citizens are theoretically at risk of denaturalization or the revocation of their naturalized citizenship. When might immigrants be at risk of losing United States citizenship?

When there’s proof of fraud

Typically, denaturalization occurs in response to immigration fraud. If the immigrant entered the country, adjusted their status or naturalized by misrepresenting their identity or their circumstances, that fraudulent misrepresentation could cost them their citizenship.

Those accused of illegal procurement, meaning they never met the standards for naturalization, could eventually face a review of their records. Anyone who hid material facts when interacting with immigration authorities could be at risk of denaturalization.

When there’s a connection to a subversive group

Citizens have the right to assemble peacefully, but naturalized citizens should avoid interacting with groups viewed as subversive or extreme. Joining totalitarian or Communist parties or associating with terrorist organizations can lead to denaturalization.

Finally, those who gain immigration opportunities through military service could be at risk as well. If they receive a discharge other than an honorable one before five years of service, their citizenship could be at risk.

Immigrants concerned about their legal status may need support even after naturalization. Responding appropriately to allegations of immigration fraud or other misconduct can help people remain in the United States permanently.

title: Which immigrants receive conditional green cards?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: A green card is a permanent resident card. It identifies an individual as a foreign national who has long-term authorization to remain in the United States. Although the name of the document implies that it lasts indefinitely, a green card is typically only valid for one decade. Permanent residents need to renew their green cards…
content:
A green card is a permanent resident card. It identifies an individual as a foreign national who has long-term authorization to remain in the United States. Although the name of the document implies that it lasts indefinitely, a green card is typically only valid for one decade. Permanent residents need to renew their green cards every 10 years in most cases.

Occasionally, their green cards may last for a shorter period because they are conditional. What circumstances might lead to immigrants receiving conditional green cards instead of a traditional, 10-year green card?

Investors and spouses may receive conditional status

Some people secure permanent resident status by investing in an existing business or starting a new company in the United States. They may receive conditional green cards that they must renew within two years. To do that, they must prove that their investments continue to create or preserve full-time job opportunities.

New spouses of citizens who seek green cards also receive conditional green cards. If the marriage has not already lasted more than two years, then they receive a conditional green card instead of a standard one. They must then petition to remove their conditional status. That process requires proving that they are still in the marriage that helped them obtain the green card.

After removing the conditional status, both investors and spouses no longer have to continue to fulfill the requirements imposed on them to obtain the conditional green card. If spouses divorce or the business fails, the immigrant can potentially still remain in the country legally.

Learning more about conditional green cards and appropriately adjusting them when doing so is an option can help permanent residents remain in the country indefinitely.

title: What happens when you don’t have an estate plan?
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Life has a way of staying busy, and planning for the future often slips to the bottom of the list. Many people assume their loved ones will “just know” what to do if something happens, or that everything will naturally work itself out. Unfortunately, when there is no estate plan in place, the law steps…
content:
Life has a way of staying busy, and planning for the future often slips to the bottom of the list. Many people assume their loved ones will “just know” what to do if something happens, or that everything will naturally work itself out.

Unfortunately, when there is no estate plan in place, the law steps in and makes those decisions for you. Those default rules may look nothing like what you would have wanted, and they can create stress and conflict at an already emotional time.

How intestate succession decides your estate for you

When someone dies without a valid will or trust, they are considered to have died “intestate.” In that situation, state intestate succession laws control who inherits property, how much they receive and in what order. These laws are rigid and leave no room for personal preferences, family dynamics or special circumstances.

Typically, intestate succession prioritizes close legal relatives. A surviving spouse and children often inherit first, but the exact division depends on state law and family structure. Blended families, long-term partners who are not legally married and stepchildren are especially vulnerable under these rules, as they may receive nothing at all.

If there is no spouse or children, the estate may pass to parents, siblings, or more distant relatives. In rare cases where no qualifying relatives can be found, the estate can even escheat to the state. None of these outcomes take emotional bonds, promises or intentions into account.

Beyond who inherits, intestate estates often take longer to settle. Court involvement is usually required, and a personal representative may be appointed who is not the person you would have chosen. This can increase costs, delays and the likelihood of disputes among family members during probate. An estate plan is about more than wealth. Without one, there are no instructions for guardianship of minor children, no guidance for managing assets responsibly and no way to protect loved ones with special needs or unique circumstances.

A thoughtfully prepared plan allows you to make decisions intentionally, reduce uncertainty, and give clarity to the people you care about most. Speaking with a knowledgeable legal professional can help you understand your options and create a plan that reflects your values, not just the default rules of the law.

title: Trusts and blended families
author: Cynthia I. Waisman
excerpt: Blended families are often built on a foundation of love, resilience and the hope of creating something lasting together. At the same time, they can often bring unique legal and emotional considerations that require thoughtful planning. When children, stepchildren and new spouses are all part of the picture, even well-intentioned decisions can lead to uncertainty…
content:
Blended families are often built on a foundation of love, resilience and the hope of creating something lasting together. At the same time, they can often bring unique legal and emotional considerations that require thoughtful planning.

When children, stepchildren and new spouses are all part of the picture, even well-intentioned decisions can lead to uncertainty. Clear planning can help preserve harmony and protect the people who matter most.

Planning with care for a blended family

A Trust is a legal arrangement where a grantor transfers assets to a trustee to benefit a beneficiary. The grantor can appoint a neutral trustee, set rules for decision-making and create safeguards for younger beneficiaries or those who may need long-term support. For blended families, this level of customization often provides peace of mind that informal plans simply cannot match.

Trusts are often a powerful tool for blended families because they allow for clarity, structure and control. Without a trust, assets may pass automatically under state law or beneficiary designations in ways that unintentionally disinherit children from a prior relationship. A carefully drafted trust can specify how and when assets are distributed, reducing confusion and minimizing the risk of disputes after death.

Trusts also offer protection against challenges and misunderstandings. When expectations are clearly documented, there is less room for interpretation or resentment. Provisions can address issues such as unequal inheritances, shared property or future changes in family structure, all while maintaining privacy and flexibility that a simple will may not be able to provide.

Planning ahead is not about anticipating conflict, but about preventing it. A trust can serve as a stabilizing framework that honors relationships, protects children and reflects the family’s values. If you’re navigating the complexities of a blended family, seeking legal guidance from a professional can help ensure your wishes are clearly defined and your loved ones are protected for the future.
